reason: The sources provide multi-site verification for over a dozen dramatic, surprising facts covering the spacewalk crisis, reentry failures, and survival in the taiga.
story: On March 18, 1965, Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov made history on Voskhod 2 by performing humanity's first spacewalk. But the triumph quickly became a brush with death. In the vacuum of space, Leonov's spacesuit ballooned and stiffened so severely that his boots and gloves slipped off his limbs, leaving him unable to fit into the airlock. Facing suffocation within minutes as the capsule hurtled into orbital darkness, Leonov broke protocol by bleeding off his suit's oxygen below safety limits without alerting ground control, desperately wrestling back inside head-first. Back aboard, their guidance system failed, forcing a manual reentry burn. The orbital module failed to detach cleanly, sending the craft into a violent ten-G spin before burning free. Voskhod 2 crash-landed deep in the snow-covered Ural taiga, where Leonov and crewmate Pavel Belyayev spent two freezing nights surrounded by bears and wolves before ski rescuers arrived.
angle: To survive the first spacewalk in history, Alexei Leonov had to secretly vent his spacesuit's oxygen below safety limits just to squeeze back through the airlock door.

claims.claim: On March 18, 1965, Alexei Leonov became the first human to conduct a spacewalk.
The historic mission was Voskhod 2, crewed by pilot Alexei Leonov and commander Pavel Belyayev.
Leonov began his spacewalk roughly 90 minutes after launch.
Leonov floated outside the spacecraft tethered by a line for approximately 12 minutes.
In the vacuum of outer space, Leonov's spacesuit ballooned and stiffened until he could no longer bend his joints or re-enter the airlock.
Due to the suit ballooning, Leonov's hands slipped out of his gloves and his feet slipped out of his boots.
To squeeze back inside, Leonov had to open a valve and bleed off suit pressure below safety limits, risking decompression sickness and oxygen starvation.
Leonov decided not to report his pressure bleeding maneuver to ground control over the radio.
Leonov entered the airlock head-first rather than feet-first, in violation of standard operating procedure.
Soviet state radio and television suspended live broadcasts from the mission once problems developed.
While on the Voskhod 2 flight, Leonov created the first artwork drawn in space by sketching an orbital sunrise with colored pencils.
During reentry, the automated landing guidance system malfunctioned, forcing the crew to pilot a manual retrofire.
The landing module failed to separate cleanly from the orbital module on schedule, tethered by a cable that sent the spacecraft into a violent spin until about 100 kilometers altitude.
The landing craft touched down far off course in deep snow within the heavily forested Ural Mountains region.
The crew was stranded in the taiga during the mating season of local bears and wolves, armed with a survival pistol and ammunition.
Rescue helicopters could not land due to dense forest, and an immediate airlift using a rope ladder was ruled out.
Nighttime temperatures dropped to minus 22 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 30 degrees Celsius) while the cosmonauts were stranded.
Rescuers arrived on skis and constructed a small log cabin and an enormous fire to shelter the crew.
After spending two cold nights in the forest, the cosmonauts skied approximately 9 kilometers to an extraction helicopter.
A decade later in 1975, Leonov commanded the Soviet Soyuz 19 capsule for the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project, docking with an American Apollo spacecraft.

disputed: The exact length of the spacewalk tether varies across accounts, with some sources listing 5.35 meters (17.6 feet) and others listing 4.8 meters (16 feet); scripts should generalize or specify according to one record.

The distance the capsule overshot its landing zone differs considerably, ranging from 386 km (240 mi) to over 600 miles or 1,500 to 2,000 km in Leonov's personal recollections; scripts should attribute the variance ('landing hundreds of miles off course').

Accounts differ on whether the rope ladder rescue was rejected by aviation commanders as too hazardous or attempted and aborted by the cosmonauts because their stiff suits made climbing impossible; scripts should attribute both viewpoints.
